transcript.text: I run a roofing company dealing about
3.1 million a year and I want to hit 6
million, but I've never had a real
manager between me and my crews. I can't
afford to bring an outsider at a 90
grand and have it flop. How do you make
that first operator hire when you can't
afford to get it wrong?
>> Really good question.
So, if the margin for error in the
business is this small, so $100,000 a
year on 3.1 million,
I would actually look at the model
itself and think that we might have a
pricing and sales motion issue before
having an operator issue. Basically like
if the business requires an all-star in
order to make it work, the model is
broken. And that happens across all
businesses. And so, for you, I would fix
pricing and sales motion first, increase
the cash in the business, so that I can
then make sure that this person who
comes in doesn't make or break the
business. That's thing one. When this
person does come in, you can pull them
from the outside, but sometimes if you
promote from within, there might be no
one who has the leadership skills to
have the respect of the guys. Now, I'm
an always an advocate if you can't
promote from within, do so. But at the
end of the day, there are a set of
skills that are required to lead. If
that person cannot model what good looks
like, define it clearly in terms of
behaviors, and do it in front of them,
get them to try to do it, see what they
do, give corrective feedback in the
moment when they get it wrong, and give
praise when they get it right, and then
continue to do it day in and day out,
then they're not going to be a leader.
And so, what I would look for is who on
the team is the most extreme example of
the standards that I want to set. If no
one on the team embodies those
standards, then I would look for someone
else who does, and I would make it clear
to that person that your job is to model
perfection.
